en: The Treatise on the Eighteen Emptinesses, which is also sixteen, eighteen, fourteen, and seventeen,
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Question:
Emptiness is without differentiation; how can there be eighteen kinds? Answer:

To reveal that the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—are the universal characteristic of all dharmas, they are now categorized into eighteen types based on the different classes of phenomena. What are these?

1. Internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), 2. external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), 3. internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), 4. great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), 5. emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), 6. emptiness of reality (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), 7. emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), 8. emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), 9. ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), 10. emptiness of that which has no before or after (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), 11. emptiness of non-abandonment (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), 12. emptiness of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu-śūnyatā*), 13. emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), 14. emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), 15. emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), 16. emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), 17. emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and 18. emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
Combining these eighteen [emptinesses] results in sixteen emptinesses; they are established as sixteen emptinesses for two reasons:
first, essence (tǐ);
second, function (yòng).
The first is internal emptiness, also called the emptiness of the experiencer.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles regard the six sense bases as the experiencer, because they are able to experience the retributive fruits of the six objects.
Now it is clarified that there are only the six sense faculties and no agent of grasping; because there is no grasping, it is said that the experiencer is empty.
Second is the emptiness of the external, also called the emptiness of the experienced.
Apart from the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*), there is no separate dharma that can be experienced.

If all that sentient beings receive and employ are merely the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and since there is no internal person who can experience them and no external dharma that can be experienced, then both person and dharma are empty.
Because consciousness alone exists and there is no external object, it is called "emptiness of the external.
Because there is no object, there is likewise no consciousness; this is "emptiness of the internal.
That the six sense bases lack consciousness is precisely the absence of a person.
The absence of sense faculties and their objects constitutes the non-existence of phenomena.
Thus, the two meanings of internal and external emptiness mutually establish one another.
Third is internal-external emptiness, which refers to the emptiness of the body.

This body, composed of the four great elements, serves as the basis for both the internal and the external; the internal basis refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Since the five physical faculties all possess translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), and the mental faculty (*manas*) likewise relies upon this body, they are collectively termed the "internal basis."

The external basis refers to the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhyaviṣaya*). As for one's own body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), with the exception of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) which are pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*), all remaining forms, odors, and so forth belong to the six external sense objects. They are called "external" because they are supported by the five sense faculties, not because they exist outside the body.
This body can sustain the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and is therefore called the "basis," for it is that upon which the organs and objects depend.
Since both these organs and what are not organs are entirely empty, it is called "internal and external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
The fourth is the great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), which refers to that upon which the body relies, namely the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).
Because the ten directions are all immeasurable and boundless emptiness, it is called the great emptiness.

The fifth is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). It is able to illuminate the characteristics of reality by synthesizing the preceding four types of emptiness; because it is named after its object, it is called "emptiness-wisdom" (*śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Since this emptiness-wisdom is itself empty, the "emptiness of emptiness" is established.
The sixth is true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*), which refers to the emptiness of the true object.

When the practitioner perceives that both the internal and external are empty—neither person nor phenomenon existing—this object is truly real. It is established as "true" by virtue of its being the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); because this nature cannot be apprehended, it is called the nature of discrimination, and the emptiness of this nature is precisely true emptiness.
These six types of emptiness establish the nature of emptiness through their own internal sequence:

first, the emptiness of the experiencer; second, the emptiness of the experienced object; third, the emptiness of one's own body; fourth, the emptiness of the place where the body dwells; fifth, the emptiness of the illuminating subject; and sixth, the emptiness of the observed object.

The first four are all the emptiness of the objects of observation; the fifth is the emptiness of the observing wisdom; and the sixth is the emptiness of the characteristics of the objects being discriminated.
Furthermore, the first four are the objects of knowledge, the fifth is the knowing subject, and the sixth is the characteristics of the objects of knowledge.
The fifth wisdom, which is emptiness (*jñāna-śūnyatā*), remedies the four preceding objects; these four objects are empty.
The sixth is true emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā*), which remedies the fifth wisdom, whereby wisdom becomes empty.

If there were no fifth wisdom of emptiness to remedy the four preceding objects, then there would be a person and dharmas, which constitute the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
By means of this wisdom and vision, one realizes that the objects before one are neither persons nor phenomena; this constitutes the treatment of those objects.

If there were no sixth object—the emptiness that treats the fifth wisdom—this wisdom would be merely a true understanding and would thus revert to being of a discriminative nature. Therefore, it is said that the sixth, true emptiness, is called "treative wisdom."
The second meaning, the elucidation of emptiness, consists of twelve points:
first, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*);

second, the emptiness of non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskāra-śūnyatā*). The Bodhisattva studies these two types of emptiness in order to attain two kinds of wholesome dharmas: first, the wholesome path; second, the wholesome fruit.
The "Path" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth; "wholesome fruits" refer to bodhi and so forth.
One who practices emptiness clarifies that the various paths of the three vehicles are devoid of a person or dharmas, being neither real nor illusory.
To be free from these four kinds of mind is called the virtuous cause.
To attain this virtuous cause, the Bodhisattva practices the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Those who practice emptiness attain two kinds of virtuous fruits, namely *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
If there is a remainder of the origin [of suffering], this fruit is separated from the four kinds of perversions and is not permanent, blissful, self, or pure.
If there is the remainderless cessation of suffering, it is precisely permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
These seventh and eighth types of emptiness constitute the purification of the bodhisattva’s own self-deliverance: first attaining the Path and subsequently attaining the fruit.

The third, ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), is for the sake of constantly benefiting others; the bodhisattva cultivates this ultimate emptiness so as to constantly desire to benefit others until all sentient beings are exhausted, vowing to perpetually transform them.
This mind possesses attachments.

Now, regarding this contemplation of the mind: this mind must certainly cause one to relinquish the ultimate mind; when it spontaneously benefits others, that is true wisdom, which is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
If one acts with a resolute mind, one can bring about benefit; if one does not act, there is no benefit.
It is no longer merely spontaneous, but constantly benefits others without fail.
This resolute mind is the ninth wisdom, called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
The fourth is the emptiness of no before or after, also called the emptiness of no beginning.
It is established for the sake of perfecting ultimate emptiness and benefiting others.
That which has no before or after is without beginning or end.
If a bodhisattva does not understand that these are empty, they will give rise to a mind of weariness and aversion, abandoning birth and death.
Once they see that birth and death are empty, they do not differentiate between before and after, nor between beginning and end.

Since one no longer discriminates between beginning and end, the mind is free from sorrow or joy regarding the short or the long; one does not grieve over the long, nor does one rejoice upon hearing of the short.
Having abandoned both sorrow and joy, one is then able to remain without forsaking birth and death.
Because of this non-abandonment, ultimate benefit is finally accomplished. For this reason,
the tenth is the contemplation of the emptiness of no-beginning,
and the fifth is the emptiness of non-abandonment.
When Bodhisattvas practice and study this samādhi of cessation, it is for the sake of making their roots of merit and goodness inexhaustible. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas, even within *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, do not abandon the gateway of roots of merit and goodness.
Although the retributive fruits of the outflows have been exhausted, because the roots of merit and virtue serve to transform sentient beings, this function remains constant.

Thus, even though the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, he still manifests the two bodies—the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and the transformation-body (saṃbhogakāya)—in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings to guide and benefit all conscious beings; this is precisely the meaning of "arousing the mind once again."
Therefore, as long as sentient beings are not yet exhausted, the functioning of their responsive transformations will likewise never be exhausted.
Thus it is said that although they have entered the realm of Nirvana without remainder, they do not abandon their roots of merit and virtue.
If those of the two vehicles enter extinction, they no longer give rise to the thought [of awakening], because their compassion is meager and they do not transform sentient beings.

If a Buddha were to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and yet further give rise to a mind, it is because the three bodies (*trikāya*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings without end; and because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the locus of all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, it is said that even upon dissolution, one does not abandon or depart from these merits.
The reason we know that the Dharma-body still exists within nirvana is because it constitutes the ultimate essence.
Since the functioning of the manifested response is seen to be inexhaustible, we know that the essence of this body is eternally serene and forever free from transition or decay.
As the Vaibhāṣika masters say, nirvāṇa lacks intrinsic characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), yet it cannot be said to be non-existent.
Why? Because it is capable of manifesting functional efficacy (kāryakriyā).
If one does not rely on nirvana, wisdom will not be perfected; if wisdom is not perfected, then afflictions will not be extinguished.
Since nirvana can give rise to the Path, and the Path can extinguish delusions, this is precisely the internal affair of nirvana.
Since we perceive that there are phenomena, we know that they must have a substantial basis; therefore, one cannot say they do not exist.
The same principle applies to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body within nirvāṇa.

To eliminate conceptualization while not abandoning merit is precisely the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); since this conceptualization does not exist within the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), it is called "emptiness that is not abandoned."

In language, one speaks of nirvāṇa as not abandoning merit; yet within nirvāṇa itself, there is no intention of not abandoning. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of non-abandonment, which constitutes the meaning of not abandoning saṃsāra.
Previously, it was clarified that not abandoning birth-and-death for the sake of ultimate benefit to others distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from the Two Vehicles, whose benefit cannot be eternal;

now, it is clarified that although they abide in both birth-and-death and nirvana, they transform sentient beings in both states, and since this principle remains unchanged, we have arrived at this point.
There are three kinds of emptiness that are termed "benefiting others," which constitute the eleventh, the non-abandonment of emptiness, also known as the non-diffusion of emptiness.
The sixth, the emptiness of nature; the seventh, the emptiness of characteristics; and the eighth, the emptiness of all phenomena—these three clarify the causes for benefiting oneself and others.
Question:
For what purpose is emptiness? Answer:
Because the pure Buddha-nature is itself emptiness, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Question:
For what reason is it called "emptiness of nature"?
Answer: Buddha-nature is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Why is this so?
Because it exists naturally.
However, "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) has two meanings:
first, beginninglessness; second, causality.
For example, within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, both the mind and the non-mind are naturally without cause.
If the mind were to have a cause, would this cause be inherently existent?
Does it begin to exist?
If there is an original cause, then that cause must be spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Since it is spontaneous, one must also admit that the mind is spontaneous.

In the past, when there was no cause, there should have been no sentient beings; it is only when there is a cause at a certain time that sentient beings exist, as in the case of earth, stones, and so forth.
If there were a cause, they should have become sentient beings [at that time].

Therefore, we know that a portion of *svabhāva* (nature) produces the state of having consciousness, while another portion produces the state of being without consciousness; hence it is said that, for example, within beginningless birth and death, the two dharmas of having consciousness and being without consciousness are naturally so without cause.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; it is spontaneous and without cause.
If even that which is false possesses the meaning of spontaneity, how much more so must that which is true be spontaneous?
Therefore, it takes the beginningless Buddha-nature as its cause.
Therefore, those within the six sense bases who seek liberation will not achieve the fruit of liberation if they lack Buddha-nature; it is like a pure jewel that can clarify turbid water.
Because buddha-nature is beginningless, the beginninglessness of birth and death is empty of identity and difference.
The emptiness of the pure and the impure is as explained above.
This nature of emptiness serves to eliminate five faults and manifest five kinds of merit.
The person and phenomena are the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The arising of conceptualization from the person and phenomena is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

When one seeks phenomena within the nature of conceptualization, they are unobtainable; when one seeks the person and phenomena that are conceptually constructed within the dependent nature, they too are unobtainable—this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Ultimate reality is without substance; because it is without substance, it is without characteristics; because it is without characteristics, it is without arising; because it is without arising, it is without cessation; because it is without cessation, it is quiescent; and this quiescence is itself the nirvana of intrinsic nature.
This emptiness of intrinsic nature eliminates five kinds of faults:

first, it eliminates the inferior mind. If one does not have sufficient faith that the Buddha-nature exists and can be attained, and that its attainment brings immeasurable merit, then one cannot generate the bodhicitta. Without generating this mind, one will constantly remain in an inferior state.
Because the Buddha-nature causes one to resolve upon enlightenment, it is said that it can eliminate the inferior mind.

Second, it eliminates the arrogant mind: if a person does not understand the equality of the Buddha-nature, they may think, "I possess the Buddha-nature and have already resolved upon enlightenment, whereas others lack the Buddha-nature and cannot resolve upon enlightenment," and thus become conceited.
If one realizes this principle, there is neither "this" nor "that," and the haughty mind is immediately extinguished; thus, it is said that one can eliminate haughtiness.

Third, eliminating attachment to the false and abandoning the real: the reason why the false constitutes the faults of saṃsāra is as follows—when someone comes to strike, beat, revile, or insult one, these things (1) do not exist inherently from the beginning, and (2) arise through the activity of the mind and the production of the false.
That which is not natural is, in itself, false and illusory.

If one does not realize the principle of ultimate reality, yet claims this [illusory state] to be real, one will cling to the false and abandon the true; thus, the sharp afflictions such as the three poisons arise.

If one realizes that birth and death are illusory and not substantially existent, then one will no longer perceive the one who strikes or the one who reviles, will no longer see the faults of sentient beings, and will not give rise to afflictions; thus, one abandons all that is illusory.
To see that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that their merits are perfectly equal is itself the grasping of reality; from this, one gives rise to compassion and becomes a Bodhisattva.
Fourth, it can eliminate the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). All phenomena are, from the very beginning, true in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); whether they exist or do not exist, both are equal.
If a person can form this understanding, they will immediately abandon the mind that clings to signs through the view of self.
Fifth, by eliminating fear, one can cause sentient beings to believe in and accept the profound True Dharma.

The True Dharma consists of both the characterized and the uncharacterized; if one realizes the Buddha-nature, one will be able to believe in and accept the uncharacterized True Dharma, and thus will not slander the Mahāyāna.

Next, to clarify how this emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) can induce five kinds of merit: first, it eliminates inferiority and gives rise to right diligence; second, it eliminates arrogance and gives rise to equanimity; third, it eliminates delusion and gives rise to compassion; fourth, it eliminates [wrong] views and gives rise to *prajñā*; and fifth, because one eliminates fear and accepts the true Dharma, it is called the emptiness of nature.

The revelation of the principle of Buddha-nature possesses five kinds of merit and is free from five faults; by treating and protecting this nature so that it attains purity, it serves as the cause for self-benefit. Therefore, this twelfth [chapter] is named "Nature-Emptiness" (svabhāva-śūnyatā).
The Buddha-nature is emptiness itself.
The seventh is the emptiness of self-characteristics, which serves to attain the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks.
Furthermore, these marks are of two kinds:
First is the form-aspect, which refers to the four great elements and the five sense objects;
second is the formless-aspect, which refers to all four aggregates that are mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
The transformation body is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
Why is this? Birth and death are false and inverted, not exceeding the two truths of suffering and its origin; the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not so.

Because it exists in accordance with the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), its substance is non-inverted, and furthermore, it can eliminate the inversions of sentient beings; therefore, it is said to be "not birth and death."
That which is not nirvāṇa has a beginning and an end.
Because it is not saṃsāra, it lacks the illusory characteristics of birth and death;
because it is not nirvāṇa, it likewise lacks the real characteristics of nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

If a bodhisattva is able to cultivate this emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), they cause the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs to be purified as the very characteristics of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); therefore, the thirteenth is named the emptiness of marks.

Regarding the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*): it refers to the immeasurable *Ganges-sand* number of dharmas of all Tathāgatas—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth—which are empty in that their luminous characteristics are neither separate nor inseparable.
If one considers the Dharma-body in relation to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), there is both separation and non-separation.
However, when the response-body disappears, it does not separate from the Dharma-body.
Why? Because they are one.
The Dharma-body is the root and the response-body is the branch; the branch does not depart from the root, yet the root is not separated from the branch.
Question:
If the Dharma-body does not depart from the response-body, what fault would there be?
Answer: If that were so, then when one person attains Buddhahood, all people should likewise attain it.
Since all people do not attain it simultaneously, we know that the Dharma-body possesses the meaning of not being identical to the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The Dharma-body is likewise not separate from the Response-body. Why is this?
Because the Dharma-body is without differentiation and is eternally inseparable from the merits of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If one can practice in such a way—neither adhering to nor departing from the principle—then one will attain the fruit of the *sāmbhogakāya*.

Both the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *sāmbhogakāya* are capable of benefiting sentient beings: the *nirmāṇakāya* primarily plants the seeds, while the *sāmbhogakāya* brings them to maturity, causing this emptiness of all phenomena to become the purification of all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas possess two further meanings:
first, there is neither separation nor non-separation, because one must not engage in partial attachment;
second, there is neither the grasper nor the grasped, because there is no distinction between the object and the wisdom that cognizes it.
This concludes the fourteenth [section], the analysis of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
Up to this point, there have been three types of emptiness, which complete the explanation of the causes for benefiting oneself and others.

The fifteenth is the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*) and the sixteenth is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*); these two emptinesses generally emerge from the essence of the preceding fourteen emptinesses.
To speak of the "emptiness of existing phenomena" means that both the person and phenomena are non-existent, intended to eliminate the slander of overestimation (*samāropa*).
To speak of the "emptiness of non-existing phenomena" means that they truly exist.

This principle of the non-existence of persons and phenomena removes the false attachments of sentient beings; because they claim that this principle does not exist, it is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), which serves to eliminate the slander of nihilism (*apavāda*).
Being free from increase and free from decrease, it is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is called the essence of emptiness.
Thus, these two types of emptiness are themselves subsumed within the preceding fourteen kinds of emptiness.
Seventeenth is the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāva-abhāva-śūnyatā*); this single emptiness gives rise to the characteristics of all other emptinesses.

As for what is called the emptiness of existence and non-existence, it clarifies that the essential nature and characteristic of this emptiness are definitively non-existent, which is precisely termed "definitive non-existence."
Because there is this principle of the non-existence of persons and the existence of dharmas, it is called "definitively existent.
This non-existence and this existence constitute the essential characteristic of emptiness.
The essence clarifies that, in principle, there is neither increase nor decrease; the characteristic clarifies that its essence is definitive.

To determine that something is non-existent or to determine that it is existent is precisely to regard it as truly non-existent or truly existent; yet, in truth, there are neither persons nor dharmas, and in truth, this principle exists.
The reason this treatise explains only sixteen kinds of emptiness is precisely because these two [final] kinds of emptiness are subsumed within the essence of the preceding six kinds of emptiness.
Furthermore, they are also considered fourteen kinds of emptiness because the latter four kinds of emptiness further analyze the essential characteristics of the preceding ones.
Since this subsequent emptiness is subsumed within the preceding fourteen types, there are variations in the detailed and abbreviated enumerations of fourteen, sixteen, and eighteen.
The eighteenth [type] brings forth the fruit of emptiness; as for what is called "emptiness of the unobtainable," it clarifies that this fruit is difficult to attain.
Why is this? Because this principle of emptiness is neither annihilated nor eternal, yet it is precisely the Great Eternal.
Since the meaning of "eternal" cannot be apprehended, the meaning of "annihilated" likewise cannot be apprehended.
Because no fixed characteristic can be apprehended, it is called "difficult to attain. Why is this?
This principle of emptiness is neither suffering nor pleasure, yet it is great bliss; it is neither self nor non-self, yet it is the Great Self; it is neither pure nor impure, yet it is great purity.

This emptiness is subsumed under the functional applications of the eight types of emptiness; because the non-existence of persons and phenomena is precisely the essence of emptiness, it is called "conforming to the differences in functional applications," wherein distinctions are established through their various manifestations.
As explained above, the first six emptinesses clarify the essence of emptiness, while the [subsequent] ten emptinesses clarify the function of emptiness.

Within these functions, the final two emptinesses are subsumed under the fourteen emptinesses; the seventeenth single emptiness is subsumed under the essence of the six emptinesses, and the eighteenth single emptiness is subsumed under the function of the eight emptinesses. Thus, the eighteen become sixteen, and the sixteen revert to fourteen.

Sometimes the broad comes first and the concise follows; sometimes the concise comes first and the broad follows. Whether the principle and the phenomenon differ, or whether their essence and characteristics are distinct, the meaning of their separation or unification is as described here.
Below this, the fourth section, the analysis of the principle of emptiness, has three parts:
first, purity and impurity.
If one were to say that emptiness is definitively impure, then all sentient beings would be unable to attain liberation.
Why is this? Because that which is definitively impure cannot be made pure.
If one were to say that it is definitively pure, then the cultivation of the path would be useless.

Why is this? Because even before attaining the untainted path of liberation, the essence of emptiness is inherently and naturally pure; thus, there are no afflictions that can act as obstacles to wisdom.
Furthermore, if it were possible to remove [defilements] without relying on effort, all sentient beings would attain liberation spontaneously.
We observe, however, that sentient beings do not attain liberation without effort; thus, we know that this emptiness is not inherently pure.
Furthermore, since liberation is attained through deliberate effort, one knows that this emptiness is not definitively impure.
This is called the principle of the pure-impure and the impure-pure.
Another explanation:
If one were to say that the principle of emptiness is definitively impure, then all effort and exertion would be without fruit or reward. Why is this so?

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is impure, even if a path were produced, it could not remove this impurity in the conventional sense, and thus the path would be useless.
Since this is not the case, we know that this emptiness is not impure by nature.
Question:
If that is so, since there is no intrinsic impurity, there should likewise be no intrinsic purity.
How then can the dharmadhātu be distinguished as being neither pure nor impure?
Answer:

The amala-vijñāna is the intrinsically pure mind; however, it is called "impure" because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions, and it is established as "pure" when those adventitious afflictions are exhausted.
Question:
Why is it not stated that [the mind] is definitively pure or definitively impure, but rather that it is "either pure or impure"? Answer:
This is to clarify that the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* differs from that of the five sense bases (*āyatana*) and the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
The reason it is not described as "pure" is to demonstrate that although the eyes and other faculties are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are not defiled by those afflictions.
Furthermore, it is not pure, nor is it pure by nature; therefore, it is not described as pure.
If it is the *dharmadhātu*, although it is shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not defiled by those afflictions; thus, it is not impure, but is pure by nature.
Because it is pure by its very nature (*svabhāva*), it is not said to be impure.
Thus, one should know that the *dharmadhātu* is essentially distinct from the five sense bases (*pañcāyatana*).
Question:
Why is it not stated that this is definitively impure?
Answer: It is in order to clarify that it differs from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Why is this? If one were to say that the dharma-dhātu definitely possesses afflictions, then its intrinsic nature would be impure.
However, although this dharma-dhātu is obscured by afflictions, it is not impure by intrinsic nature; therefore, it cannot be said to be definitively impure.
It is not that it is impure; rather, it is precisely the principle of the *dharmadhātu* that exists as a certainty.
Question:
Why is it not said that suchness (*tathatā*) is definitively pure, yet is described as both pure and impure?
Answer: It is taught as pure or impure for the sake of causing sentient beings to cultivate the path;
this reveals that suchness (tathatā) is distinct from the five faculties.
Why is this? Because suchness and the five faculties are equally covered by afflictions, yet neither is defiled by them; they are equally pure, though the meaning of their purity differs.
Why is this? Because the essence of the five faculties is free from afflictions and does not possess the nature of afflictions; thus, the five faculties are purely pure and not impure.
If suchness were not free from afflictions and were instead the self-nature of afflictions, then one would know that purity possesses the further meaning of impurity.

Furthermore, just as Suchness (*tathatā*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are both covered by afflictions and thus share the quality of being impure, their meanings of "impurity" are nonetheless different.
If it is meditative concentration, being covered by afflictions and further defiled, it loses its own nature entirely; its entire substance becomes affliction and becomes unwholesome (*akuśala*).

If it is suchness (tathatā), although it is called impure because it is not separate from afflictions, it nevertheless does not lose its intrinsic nature, nor does it transform into afflictions or unwholesome states.
To say that what is impure also possesses the meaning of purity can be expressed in three propositions:
first, when the five sense faculties are free from afflictions and are not defiled by them, they are merely pure and not impure.
The second dhyāna-samādhi constitutes affliction; being defiled by afflictions, it is merely impure and possesses no further purity.
The third, suchness (tathatā), is pure because it differs from the five sense faculties and is not defiled by afflictions;
yet, because it is not separate from afflictions, it is simultaneously impure.
Therefore, it is said that while it is pure, there is also the meaning of impurity.
Furthermore, because suchness is distinct from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it does not depart from afflictions; thus it is said to be impure.
Yet, as it does not lose its own nature, nor does it transform into afflictions or unwholesome states, it is said that while it is impure, there is also the meaning of purity.
Second, the principle of being neither existent nor non-existent is explained:
it is called "not existent" because there is no person and no dharma; it is called "not non-existent" because the principle that there is truly no person and no dharma actually exists.
To say that there is truly existence or truly non-existence is itself neither existence nor non-existence.
This clarifies the principle of being neither identical nor different.
Regarding all that is pure and impure, purity is the state of being free from both annihilationism and eternalism.
Because the meaning of "permanence" differs from the self, it is said that they are not one; because the essence of the self is permanent, it is said that they are not different.
This clarifies that suchness possesses the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding these sixteen kinds of emptiness, they are analyzed into four categories:
First, there are six kinds of emptiness, which define the intrinsic characteristics of emptiness.
Next, there are eight kinds of emptiness, which define the functional applications of emptiness.
Third, there are two kinds of emptiness, which define purity and impurity.

The Fourth Clarification states that the principle of these sixteen kinds of emptiness can eliminate four types of faults: first, it eliminates discursive proliferation; second, it eliminates fear; third, it eliminates indolence; and fourth, it eliminates doubt.
First, regarding the elimination of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there are two aspects.

First, worldly sentient beings give rise to immeasurable conceptual proliferations within internal and external phenomena, such as asserting "there is a self" or "there is no self," all of which rely upon the human path, its fruits, and so forth; this is called conceptual proliferation.
If one perceives that both the path and the fruit of the path are entirely empty, then one is able to eliminate these forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If it is internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and great emptiness—these four types of emptiness can eliminate the conceptual proliferations of the two selves (the self of persons and the self of phenomena) within the mundane world.

If it is the emptiness of emptiness and the ultimate emptiness of reality—these two types of emptiness can eliminate the conceptual proliferations regarding the objects and wisdom of supramundane cause and effect.

Second, regarding the removal of fear: when sentient beings hear that all persons are empty, they give rise to fear and are unwilling to cultivate the Path; therefore, the Tathāgata explains for their sake that this emptiness possesses functional efficacy.

Why is this? If a person can cultivate the functional application of the eight kinds of emptiness, they will be able to attain the Path and its fruits, up to and including all merits such as the three bodies.

Third, regarding the removal of indolence: if one observes that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is pure, one will not exert effort in cultivating the path; if one says that meditative concentration is impure, then it could never be eliminated, nor would there be any need to cultivate the path, resulting in remaining forever within birth and death without liberation.
Therefore, one must distinguish whether this [nature] is pure or impure.
Why? Because when there are delusions, it is impure; once delusions have been eliminated, it is then pure. Thus, one must cultivate the Path.

Fourth, regarding the removal of doubt and confusion: when those with deluded minds hear that suchness exists or does not exist, they give rise to hesitation and are unable to reach a definitive conclusion, just as one might see a tree stump and think it is a person, or call a person a tree stump.

The Buddha distinguished and clarified that the two selves—of person and phenomena—are definitively non-existent, while the principle that there is neither person nor phenomenon is definitively existent; thus, the two meanings of emptiness and existence both persist, and such a principle is able to eliminate the mind of doubt.
Third, the elucidation of the reality of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

This establishes that all phenomena are nothing but pure consciousness, wherein there is neither a doubter nor anything to be doubted; a detailed explanation is as found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
However, the meaning of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) has two aspects.

The first is the preparatory stage (*upāya*), which means that one first contemplates that there is only the *ālaya-vijñāna* and no other objects; having realized the emptiness of both object and cognition in the present, and having eliminated all deluded consciousness, this is called "preparatory consciousness-only."

Second, it clarifies the correct contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*): by dispelling and washing away the delusory consciousness-mind of birth and death along with its objects until they are entirely purified and exhausted, there remains only the *amala* pure mind.
The fourth clarifies the reality of the basis (*āśraya-tattva*), which is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The fifth is the reality of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-tattva*), which is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The sixth is the reality of purification (*viśuddhi-tattva*), which is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The seventh is the reality of correct practice, which is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Each of the Four Truths has three aspects, as has already been explained in detail elsewhere.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* clarifies that the Buddha taught seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*):
First, arising; second, characteristics; third, consciousness; fourth, reliance; fifth, wrong practice; sixth, purification; seventh, right practice.
Regarding the first, the suchness of arising: it means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely devoid of suchness.
The second is the *tathatā* of the two characteristics, which refers to the two kinds of selflessness:
that of persons and that of phenomena. The third is the *tathatā* of consciousness-only, which refers to the fact that all conditioned things are nothing but consciousness.
The fourth is the *tathatā* of the basis, which refers to the Truth of Suffering as it has been described.
The fifth is the suchness of wrong practice, which refers to the truth of origination as it has been described.
The sixth is the suchness of purification, which refers to the truth of cessation as it has been described.
The seventh is the suchness of right practice, which refers to the truth of the path as it has been described.
These seven kinds of suchness are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Since the ultimate truth is subsumed within the nature of reality (*tathatā*), they are therefore called the seven kinds of suchness.
This refers to the seven kinds of reality explained previously, as extensively detailed in the *Treatise on the Three Natures* (*Trisvabhāva-nirdeśa*).
Question:
How is it known that these seven kinds are all the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and are subsumed within the nature of reality (*tathatā*)?
Answer:
It is known that these seven kinds are all supreme and ultimate for two reasons; namely, they are the objective domain of the two types of wisdom.
That which is called "supreme" is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is that which is illuminated by the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); therefore, it is called "supreme.

That which is "most extreme" is the sphere of omniscience (*sarvajña-viṣaya*), which is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this conventional truth is illuminated by the wisdom of phenomena as they appear (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna*).
The wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The wisdom that accords with phenomena (*yāvadbhāva-jñāna*) is the subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the wisdom that accords with reality is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), while the wisdom that accords with phenomena is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).
This is solely a single wisdom that penetrates both the ultimate and the conventional;
it is the meaning of being simultaneously empty and true. It is termed "wisdom accordant with reality" and is also called "all-aspect wisdom."
If one considers this from a conventional perspective, it is called "knowledge according to the measure" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and is also termed "knowledge as all-knowledge.

Therefore, it is described as "supreme" and "ultimate," for these are the objects of these two types of knowledge—that is, what is known by both the knowledge according to reality (*yathārtha-jñāna*) and the knowledge according to the measure (*yathāpramāṇa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, there is another meaning: one should know that these seven kinds of suchness are subsumed within the nature of reality (*tathatā*). Why is this?

It is because it is clarified that all dharmas of reality are free from the false conceptualizations of identity and difference; that is to say, they are neither identical nor different, as they are free from the four types of denial (*apavāda*).
To clarify these seven kinds of suchness: it cannot be said that they are different from all phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), nor can it be said that they are not different from all phenomena.

It is said that they cannot be described as different from all phenomena, nor can they be described as not different; furthermore, they cannot be described as both different and not different, nor as neither different nor not different.

It is explained that regarding these seven kinds of suchness among all phenomena, one cannot say they exist, nor can one say they do not exist; it is likewise impossible to say they both exist and do not exist, or that they neither exist nor do not exist, because they are free from the four types of false attribution.
Furthermore, there is another way to know that [the object] exists:
namely, because it is a pure object of cognition, we know that it exists.

If there are those who can take these dharmas as objects of their minds, their minds will immediately become pure; therefore, one should know that these seven kinds of suchness are all eternally abiding, for their nature does not change at any time.
Because this is a pure realm, one should know that it is the nature of true goodness.
By this principle, it is eternally good; therefore, one should know that it is the Truth of Bliss (*sukha-satya*).
Why is this? Because it is eternal, it is blissful; because it is virtuous, it is pure.
These seven kinds of *tathatā* (suchness) are the essential nature of all phenomena.
Because it possesses this essential nature, it is called "self.
This refers precisely to the four virtues of permanence, bliss, purity, and self.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
The reason these seven kinds are termed *tathatā* (suchness), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and true nature (*bhūtatā*) is that they are of one and the same flavor.
Regarding "one arising suchness" (*eka-utpatti-tathatā*), it means that cause and effect are identical in essence, though their names differ.
Why is it said to be "one"?
Because they both exist as being dependent on others (*paratantra*).
Since the cause is dependent on others, the fruit is likewise dependent on others; the essence of this cause and fruit is precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) are designated as the "fruit" (phala); the five aggregates that are wholesome (kuśala), unwholesome (akuśala), or determinate (vyākṛta) are designated as the "cause" (hetu). Taking that which is capable of producing as the cause and that which is produced as the fruit, this is also [a case of] being the fruit in relation to what precedes it and the cause in relation to what follows it.

Therefore, we know that it is simply a single thought-moment of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) that possesses the designations of "cause" and "effect"; in essence, they have never been different, and thus are said to be of one substance, differing only in name.
Since both cause and effect rely upon others, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, their essence is not real, and thus they are called "of one taste.
That is to say, because they equally lack reality, it is called the "true suchness of arising" (*utpatti-tathatā*).

Regarding the statement that "the two [truths] have one taste": this true suchness of arising is, as it is, the dependent nature; thus, there is no truly existent arising, and it is therefore called the "true suchness of arising.
This is precisely the emptiness of the nature of non-arising, and because it is non-arising, it is of one taste.

Third, this dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) necessarily possesses the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva); since the imagined nature is the nature of signlessness (animitta-lakṣaṇa), and the nature of signlessness is the signless suchness (animitta-tathatā), this suchness of signs is of a single flavor (ekarasa).
Therefore, by means of these three meanings, it is called the "arising true thusness" (*utpatti-tathatā*).
Regarding the "characteristic true thusness" (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*):

because it reveals the universal characteristic of phenomena, the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—are the principle of the two emptinesses; this is named the universal characteristic of all phenomena, which is precisely what is called characteristic true thusness.

Regarding the suchness of the three consciousnesses: there is only consciousness and no objective realm (*viṣaya*). Because the objective realm is not established, consciousness is likewise not established.
Thus, both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are of the same nature of non-apprehensibility; therefore, it is called the suchness of consciousness.
Regarding the fourth, the *tathatā* (suchness) as the basis: it has the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of suffering as its essence.

These five aggregates serve as the locus of reliance for sentient beings; because they rely upon them to conceive of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and so forth, they are called the "basis."

The Truth of Suffering has four characteristics, namely: suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self. These four meanings are equally non-erroneous and are all termed "reality," which is precisely the reliance upon suchness (*tathatā*).
Second, these four characteristics below are all emptiness; because they are non-existent, they are all termed "reality" (*tattva*) and also depend upon *tathatā*.
The *tathatā* of the fivefold wrong practice refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Because "origination" (*samudaya*) has two meanings, it is termed *tathatā* (suchness):
first, non-erroneous suchness, which refers to the sense of being able to produce [phenomena].
This meaning is real, and thus it is the suchness of origination.
Second, both that which produces and that which is produced are non-existent; because they are non-existent, it is called the *tathatā* of false practice.
Sixth, the *tathatā* of purity refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
There are also two meanings:
first, non-erroneous *tathatā*, meaning that all four virtues are non-erroneous and are therefore called *tathatā*.
Second, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is indistinguishable from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), being the same *tathatā* in which nothing exists; thus it is named pure *tathatā*.
The seventh is the suchness of correct practice, which refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The Path is precisely *prajñā*; since *prajñā* and ignorance (*avidyā*) are diametrically opposed in their essential nature, the Path is the non-erroneous suchness.

Because the essence of the path and that of the afflictions are identical, because both are non-existent within the two kinds of emptiness, and because they are of one flavor as suchness (tathatā), it is called the suchness of right practice.
It is also called *tathatā* (Suchness), also called *yathābhūta* (As-it-is), and also called *bhūtārtha* (Reality); all these terms encompass it completely.
Regarding the reality of the ten superior knowledges (*daśa-jñāna-viśeṣa-bhūtārtha*), there are ten kinds of superior knowledge intended to eliminate ten kinds of views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*):
first, the attachment to oneness; [and so forth].
2. Grasping at the cause;
3. Grasping at the experiencer;
4. Grasping at the agent;
5. Grasping at a sovereign;
6. Grasping at a supreme being;
7. Grasping at permanence.
8. the grasping at the impure as pure;
9. the grasping at the practitioner;
10. the grasping at bondage and liberation.
The first is "clinging," which refers to establishing a single name by aggregating all phenomena; this results in falling into the view of annihilationism.

Why is this? As stated in a verse from the *Saptavāstuka-śāstra*: "Just as when a riverbank collapses, it does not return to its original state, so too, once the body has reached the cemetery, it does not come back again."
Only the sense faculties and their objects are called "sentient beings.

If the holy teaching were to say that there is a trace of a bird in the sky that can be seen upon meeting it, this refers to the worldly heterodox teachers who manifest the attachment to oneness; they claim that the body itself is the person, and that when the body perishes, the self perishes as well—thus falling into the view of nihilism.
To refute this attachment, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are established.

Although "superior wisdom" (*vijñāna*) has three meanings—namely, multiplicity, collection, and distinctness—the term "aggregate" refers to the form and mind of the three time periods collectively; therefore, it is called "many."
The collection of the matter and mind of the three periods of time is given the common name "aggregate" (skandha); thus, it is called a "collection.
Because the aggregate of matter is distinct from feeling, and the aggregate of feeling is distinct from perception and the others, they are termed "distinct"; these are known as the five aggregates.
If one understands that the five aggregates possess these three meanings, then there will be no attachment to them as being a single entity.

As for the "three periods of time," the past has already passed away, the future does not yet exist, and the present does not abide; yet all internal and external forms are collectively termed "aggregates" (*skandha*).
Three meanings are used as antidotes for three kinds of ignorance: first, metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*) and intermixture (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Regarding the first kind of ignorance:
those such as worldly people and non-Buddhists claim that the body is a single entity and that this single entity is the self or person (*pudgala*);
because they do not know that there are only the five aggregates (*skandha*) across the three periods of time, they fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

This is the view that the self is identical with the aggregates (skandhas); since the self perishes when the aggregates perish, the Buddha taught that the five aggregates across the three periods of time are many and not one, thereby refuting the attachment of those who hold to the notion of a single [self].

Second, regarding those who falsely designate [ignorance]: such as the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) like the Ulūkas, who claim that the body and its constituent parts are distinct; they thus cling to a person (pudgala) as being separate from phenomena (dharma). This is the clinging to a self apart from the aggregates (skandha), and therefore they fall into the view of eternalism (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi).
Why is this? Since the person and the dharmas are distinct, one might claim that while the aggregates (skandhas) perish, the self persists.
This arises from not understanding that the person is a mere conventional designation based on the collection of the aggregates; it is a name without intrinsic substance.
Because one is deluded by these conventional designations, they are called "ignorance of conventional designation.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that the collection of conventional designations constitutes phenomena (*dharma*), whose essence is emptiness; thus he refutes this attachment and speaks of being able to eliminate ignorance of conventional designation.

Regarding the "three characteristics being mixed with ignorance," this refers to the position held by the Sarvāstivādins, namely that within the Eightfold Noble Path, right intention and right view are both subsumed under *prajñā* (wisdom).
Because they are unable to distinguish between these two differences, this misconception arises.

Therefore, when the Sautrāntikas and Mahāyāna masters say that [the former] is due to "correct reflection" (*samyak-cintā*), they mean that because one seeks to investigate a prior principle that has not yet been definitively resolved, it still belongs to *manasikāra* (attention). Since *manasikāra* is itself a mental action (*manas-karman*), it is not subsumed under *prajñā* (wisdom);
only correct view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is designated as *prajñā*.
Generally speaking, all knowledge and vision that can penetrate and discern belongs to *prajñā*.

The same applies to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): if one cannot distinguish between feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), or perception and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and instead regards perception and feeling as a single entity, one loses their essential nature; this is therefore called "confused ignorance" (*saṃkīrṇa-avidyā*).
Because of the confusion caused by ignorance, one loses right view; having lost right view, one cannot attain liberation.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that the natures of the five aggregates are distinct, differentiating between sensation, perception, and the others.

To establish two types of characteristics—the specific and the general: the specific characteristic gives rise to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the general characteristic gives rise to inference (*anumāna*).
Question:
How are the five aggregates subsumed within the fundamental reality?
Answer: Form is of three kinds.

First is conceptualized form (*vikalpa-rūpa*), which includes such meanings as long and short, large and small, square and round; all these belong to conceptual designations (*prajñapti*) because they lack a separate intrinsic substance.
There are two kinds of form, each having its own category, just as a fruit arises from a cause.
Taking the production of fire as the cause, it produces that which belongs to the category of fire.

Since these categories are similar, they arise as the characteristics of real dharmas; they belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and are provisional. These categories are established by depending on causes, rather than through the power of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the three kinds of suchness-color (*tathatā-rūpa*): if it is a conceptualized conventional designation that is entirely without substance, this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

If it is a dependent conventional designation, although it possesses a substance, that substance is not real; because it exists in dependence upon others, this is the emptiness of [inherently existent] things (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
The substance of these two emptinesses is the ultimate reality; therefore, it is called "suchness-form" (*tathatā-rūpa*), because its intrinsic nature is suchness-form.

Suchness is designated by the term "form" because this is the form belonging to the realm of suchness; thus, it is termed "suchness-form. Just as a derivative is named after its source, one may also say that the source is designated by means of the derivative.
This reality is called "reality-as-conventionality"; since the substance of conventionality is itself emptiness, it is termed "reality.
Conventionality and emptiness are thus suchness (tathatā), and even the characteristic of reality cannot be apprehended.

Since the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is itself the three types of conventional designation (*trividha-prajñapti*) and is subsumed by these three designations, it follows by logical necessity that the other four aggregates—feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth—are likewise all subsumed by the three types of conventional designation.

Experiencing suffering and experiencing pleasure are conventional designations based on discrimination; the essence of discrimination arises from causes and conditions, and having causes and effects is dependent origination as a conventional designation.
Suchness (tathatā) is called the convention of reality.
If one can discern general characteristics and specific characteristics, this mind is perception (*saṃjñā*);
if one experiences pleasure and pain without further conceptual grasping, it is called feeling (*vedanā*).
The second is the "clinging to a creator" (*kartṛ-grāha*).
To sever this clinging, the superior knowledge of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) is established.
All those of the non-Buddhist schools universally cling to the notion that all phenomena arise because of me; this is called the clinging to a creator.
I possess nine qualities: namely, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, mindfulness, the Dharma, and non-Dharma.

These have existed within me from the beginning; from me arise the Dharma and non-Dharma. The Dharma and non-Dharma cause the mind to enter into conjunction with me. Because of this conjunction, there is cognition; because of cognition, there is pleasure; because of pleasure, there is pain. From pleasure arises desire, and from pain arises aversion. Because one desires to obtain pleasure, one loathes pain and exerts effort. Through effort, right mindfulness arises. To attain liberation, it is necessary to eliminate both the Dharma and non-Dharma.
When neither dharma nor non-dharma arises, there is no cognition; because there is no cognition, there is no suffering, pleasure, or the like.
If one seeks liberation, one should cultivate four dharmas:
first, truthful speech, which is the observance of the precepts.
Second, giving;
third, ascetic practices;
fourth, meditative concentration.

If one can cultivate these four kinds of right dharmas, one will be born into a good realm; in a good realm one attains happiness; with happiness one possesses wisdom; with wisdom one becomes weary of both the dharma and the non-dharma; being weary of both the dharma and the non-dharma, one attains liberation.
The Mahāyāna proponent says:
If it is asserted that there was previously a self but no dharmas or non-dharmas, and that at a later time these arise without causes and conditions, then liberation would be the same.
Once liberation has been attained, there should likewise be no further arising of dharmas or non-dharmas through causes and conditions; if this were the case, there would be no time of liberation.
"Element" (*dhātu*) means "seed."
One's own kind is what is called a seed (*bīja*).
Seed is also a single meaning, because its kind is identical.
It is merely by distinguishing the fruits that the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are established.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of seeds:
first, the grasper; second, the grasped; and third, the act of grasping.
The seeds of the six faculties, such as the eye, which are the graspers, are called "the category of their own seeds," meaning they are that which produces [their respective effects].
However, depending on the variations in causes and conditions, there arise fruits that differ in quality; because they vary in being superior or inferior, [the text] speaks of "seeds.
Due to past greed, karma is produced regarding the six sense objects and perfumes the *ālayavijñāna*; since the seeds are identical in being that same greed, it is referred to as "seeds."
Because this single [cause] can produce six distinct fruits for the six sense faculties (*indriya*), it is said that there are six kinds of causes.

As for the statement that the faculties are "able to grasp," since the manifest faculties are not mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), they are in reality incapable of grasping; however, because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that there is a separate person within the faculties who is the grasper, it is taught expediently that the faculties are the grasper.
The six sense objects, such as form, are that which is grasped; since seeds arise from their own seeds, it is said [they arise] from past craving.
Because the internal faculties desire to employ external objects, craving arises toward these objects by means of the faculty of craving.
Furthermore, because of craving for the six objects (*viṣaya*), there are the six sense organs (*indriya*); moreover, it is through the craving for those objects that the six organs arise.

The six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are the grasping seeds; they arise from the internal organs and external objects out of craving. These eighteen are called "elements" (*dhātu*) by virtue of their causes, for an element is a seed.
This realm is provisionally described as having three meanings:
first, the agent; second, the object of action; and third, the act itself.

When Kūṭadanta, a follower of the non-Buddhist paths, came to question the Buddha because he held the view that "I" am the agent, the Buddha employed skillful means and provisionally stated that the eyes and other faculties are the agents.

Regarding the attachment to the eyes and so forth as being the agent for the self, he further refutes the notion of a single aggregate by demonstrating that there is no distinct self apart from the sense faculties;
rather, it is merely the eyes and so forth arising from causes and conditions that are designated as "the agent," though in reality they are not agents.
The six sense objects are provisionally designated as "the produced.
This is intended to refute the two kinds of eternal self established by the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists:
the first being the conscious self, which they claim is an eternal self.
Since it is eternal, it is not an agent. The second [view] holds that the self is devoid of cognition, which is to say that all phenomena are such.
This is the self-nature of the cognizing self, accomplished through wisdom and not produced by action; it is the Buddha’s conventional designation that the six sense-objects are called "produced."
Since that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot be a real agent, one knows that objects likewise are not produced; therefore, "production" is merely a conventional designation.
Regarding these six consciousnesses: first, [this teaching] refutes the non-Buddhists who claim that all phenomena arise from a self or a mind—this is an exaggeration (samāropa).
Second, the non-Buddhist heretics with wrong views claim that the self is eternal; because the self is eternal, all phenomena are also eternal.
Since both [the self and phenomena] are thus eternally co-existent, there can be neither an agent nor an object of action; this is the slander of negation (*apavāda*).
To avoid these two extremes, it is conventionally said that the six sense objects (viṣaya) constitute "activity.

Since there is no mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the faculties (*indriya*) and objects, there is no activity; yet, apart from the faculties and objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not exist either.
Why is this? Because consciousness necessarily arises only by depending upon the sense faculties and their objects.

Thus, there is nothing that does not act [as a cause]. This is precisely to refute the three types of ignorance held by non-Buddhists—namely, the agent, the acted-upon, and so forth—and for this reason, these three meanings are established.
To reveal that seeds possess the capacity for both the grasper and the grasped, the eighteen elements (dhātus) are established.
If one understands that the eighteen elements arise from the four conditions, then one will not grasp at a self as being the producer and so forth.
The "faculties" (indriya) are termed "the agents"; there are two kinds of agency:
first, they are capable of producing consciousness; second, they are capable of acting as conditions for the objects (viṣaya).
The "objects" are termed "the acted-upon"; they act as conditions for the eye and serve as the support for consciousness.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the agent; "acting" has the sense of arising and having an object, as well as the sense of the realm (*dhātu*), originating from fundamental reality.
There are three kinds of eyes:

first, the analytical eye; second, the eye of lineage; and third, the eye of suchness. This extends up to the superior wisdom regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as explained, for example, in the section on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Fourth, in order to refute the attachment to a creator, the phenomena of cause and effect within the twelvefold dependent origination are taught; in these three meanings, there is neither increase nor decrease.
To speak of "increase or decrease" refers to establishing an unequal number of causes regarding the eleven branches, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Why is this? Because establishing the impermanent dharma as a cause for permanence is called "inequality.
For example, non-Buddhist schools such as the Sāṃkhya establish an ignorant self (*ajñātman*) as the cause.

It is also like the case of Ulūka, who posits an eternal self as the cause and clings to the eternal Lord (Īśvara) and so forth as the cause, yet is able to produce effects; this too is to posit the eternal as the cause while producing non-eternal effects. Since cause and effect are thus not analogous, it is said that the established cause is unequal (asama).

When reasoned out according to principle, the fruit of impermanence necessarily has ignorance as its cause; yet they claim there is a permanent cause, which is to say they superimpose the meaning of a cause where none exists.
Regarding the negation of causes: for example, non-Buddhist schools such as the Nirgranthas claim that all phenomena exist spontaneously and without causes or conditions.
Because they assert that what truly exists does not exist, this is called the negation of causes.

Regarding the "augmentation of the fruit" (*phalavṛddhi*): it refers to the doctrine established by the Sāṃkhyas and others, which asserts that the fruit already exists within the cause; although the fruit is inherently present, it is manifested by the cause.
Since this is claimed to be inherently existent, it would not arise from causes; yet in reality, this fruit exists only through the gathering of causes and conditions.
Because they insist that it is inherently existent, this is called "augmenting the fruit."

Regarding the "denial of the fruit" (*phalāpavāda*): it refers to the tenets established by non-Buddhist outsiders such as those with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), who claim that while all karma produces its fruit, there is no future birth.
Although there truly is fruition and truly is rebirth, they falsely maintain that these do not exist; therefore, this is called the denial of the fruit.

Regarding the augmentation of phenomena: it is as held by the followers of Maheśvara, who claim that all things arise from the mind of the Self (*ātman*), just as the entity of ignorance has a distinct mental attention (*manasikāra*) capable of producing volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, the essence of ignorance does not actually exist as something distinct that produces volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) through attention (*manasikāra*).
It is also like the position held by Ulūka, who asserts that there exists a separate activity, such as motion, apart from the substance of a phenomenon.
There are five kinds of activity (*karma*), namely: lifting, lowering, contracting, extending, and so forth; these have movement as their essence.
Apart from this essence, there is no separate activity that exists in reality, yet because it is falsely grasped as existing, it is called "superfluous activity" (*adhika-karma*).
Those who undermine the matter are the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who maintain that ignorance lacks the power to produce volitional formations (saṃskāra).
They argue that whether ignorance is present or absent, volitional formations exist spontaneously; therefore, they know that ignorance has no power to produce volitional formations.

If one understands how the twelve links of existence (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) arise in mutual succession, one can abandon the six kinds of false attachments regarding cause, effect, substance, and so forth, such as the views of increase and decrease.
Briefly explaining the meaning of the causality of the twelve links of existence, there are three aspects:
first, clarifying impermanence;
Second, to clarify the meaning of being immovable;

third, to distinguish the essence and characteristics of cause and effect: if the mind were permanent, there would be no cause and effect; because the mind is impermanent, the principle of cause and effect is established.

If one were to say that there exists a separate mental activity (manasikāra), then the cause would have to produce its fruit through mental activity, and the fruit would have to arise from the cause only after performing mental activity; this would constitute independence (svatantra) rather than dependence on others (paratantra).

Thus, the meaning of "dependent origination" arises: because the cause depends on the fruit and the fruit relies upon the cause, they are established through mutual dependence; as both are dependent, they are conventional and lack any intrinsic nature.
If they were not similar, the principle of cause and effect would be lost.
For example, beans do not produce wheat because they are not its cause; thus, things do not produce one another.

If it were allowed that the fruit does not resemble the cause and the cause is not like the fruit, then committing evil would lead to birth in heaven, while performing good deeds would cause one to fall into hell; furthermore, those with outflows (*sāsrava*) would result in liberation, and those without outflows (*anāsrava*) would further increase their cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, the impermanent gives rise to the impermanent; this follows the principle of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and does not require the exertion of intentional effort (*manasikāra*).

The similarity between cause and effect is termed the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); this teaching is intended to destroy the three types of afflictions, namely: craving as the skin, the view of self as the flesh, and ignorance as the heart.

Within the substance of these twelve links of dependent origination, if one regards those portions that are karmic retribution as truly worthy of revulsion and detachment, thereby destroying craving and attachment, this manifests the gate of liberation through wishlessness.

If it pertains to the causal aspect, it refutes the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) to reveal that the fruit arises from causes and is not produced by a permanent self, thereby clarifying the gate of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

By using ignorance (*avidyā*) to further reveal ignorance, if one can understand that all karmic formations arise from ignorance, then the mind of ignorance—which obscures—that which illuminates will be extinguished. Since ignorance is precisely the characteristic of clinging to the four types of false views, this ignorance is refuted to reveal the gate of liberation that is signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

If the substance of the twelve *bhavāṅgas* (limbs of existence) is neither increased nor decreased, then the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated; for one is thus freed from the attachment to an agent, as it is precisely these twelve *bhavāṅgas* that correctly refute this attachment.
Regarding that which is subsumed under the three natures, ignorance has three meanings:
first, that which is manifested through conceptualization, namely the conventional reality of conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva);
second, that which possesses the principle of cause and effect, namely the conventional reality of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
Both of these are non-existent; this is precisely what is meant by "conventional reality.

Since this is the case for the single factor of ignorance, the same principle applies to the remaining eleven factors, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and thus they need not be explained in detail again.
Fifth, because he refutes the attachment to Īśvara, he teaches the supreme knowledge of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).

Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that Īśvara can, according to his will, cause those who perform good to obtain the retribution of evil realms and those who produce evil to summon the fruits of the good realms; they hold that by performing actions associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), one attains liberation, and by performing actions free from outflows (*anāsrava*), one undergoes birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Why is this? Because they have attained mastery.
To refute this attachment, it is taught that both the possible (*sthāna*) and the impossible (*asthāna*) are entirely dependent on others (*paratantra*), and possess no independent mastery.
There are three meanings of "lack of sovereignty":

first, regarding what is possible and impossible in terms of karma; second, regarding what is possible and impossible in terms of afflictions; and third, regarding what is possible and impossible in terms of karmic retribution.
As explained in detail within the section on the meaning of lifespan, there are seven types of this principle of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).

Regarding the principle of possibility and impossibility with respect to karma: it is "possible" that one enters the evil realms by means of evil karma; it is not possible to enter them through the power of mastery.
If one were to rely on evil karma and yet not enter the evil realms, this would be called an impossibility; such a thing cannot exist. The same applies to wholesome karma.

Regarding those who rely on the afflictions: if a person has not abandoned the five hindrances and has not cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, they will ultimately never be able to reach the end of suffering.
Since one cannot attain liberation by relying on afflictions (*kleśa*), we know that there is no such thing as autonomous karma (*svatantra-karman*).
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are able to perform acts such as killing by relying on afflictions; however, in the absence of afflictions as a basis, they possess no power of autonomy whatsoever.
Regarding the fruit of retribution: there are no two kings in a single land, nor two Buddhas in a single world; it is impossible for two kings or two Buddhas to arise simultaneously.
Just as it is impossible for a woman to become a Wheel-Turning King, so too it is impossible for a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha of the Lesser Vehicle to become a Buddha.

Both the Wheel-Turning King and the Buddha possess uncommon karma; this karma is supreme, and by the power of all causes, conditions, and karmic retributions, even if one were to intentionally desire to be in the same place, one would ultimately not achieve it according to one's wish.
Women have two types of karma:
first, because their minds were virtuous, they obtained a human body;
second, due to evil karma, they became women, remaining perpetually subject to others and lacking self-mastery.
All of these are the retributive fruits of dependence on others.

Those of the Two Vehicles have small desires and are content; because they rely on this karma, they obtain their present fruit. Having already obtained this fruit, if they wish to seek the state of a Bodhisattva, they will ultimately be unable to attain it due to a lack of sovereign power.
This principle has two aspects:
first, based on karma; second, based on its results.

If one attains this supreme knowledge of the seven points of what is possible and what is impossible, one will be free from the view of a self and subsequently attain mastery, being able to act according to one's will.
The fundamental meaning of the three natures has already been explained as previously stated;
since similar objections can be inferred, they will not be recorded again here.
